justification: The proof is mostly sound after a suitable Y has been obtained, but it has a fatal unproven gap at the beginning. It states that one may replace D by a smooth geometrically connected F_{q^m}-rational member of the same linear system because such a member exists by Bertini and the connectedness theorem. These results are not among the supplied cited_results, and no statement, hypotheses, or proof are given. Over finite fields this is nontrivial: a smooth member over the algebraic closure is not automatically F_{q^m}-rational, and a nonempty open subset of the parameter space for |D| need not have F_{q^m}-points; a finite-field Bertini theorem (or an explicit assumption/lemma) is needed, and one must check that the linear system is very ample/separates points and tangent vectors and that the chosen divisor is defined over F_{q^m}. Without such a divisor, the q^m-arithmetic Frobenius on Y, the commutation i^*F_X=F_Yi^*, the application of the induction hypothesis to Y, and the hypothesis that Y is smooth very ample geometrically connected in the cited Lefschetz lemma are all unjustified. The geometric connectedness of Y is also asserted by an uncited connectedness theorem; the cited Lefschetz lemma and the induction hypothesis require Y to be geometrically connected, so this must be proved or properly cited. A correct proof would need to add/assume a valid existence-and-connectedness lemma for a smooth F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor in |D|, or otherwise avoid this step, before the Lefschetz, Frobenius-conjugacy, W-stability, eigenvalue, and Hermitian-form arguments can be valid.
